editor_spans.body: Beneath the language of solidarity, Britain's Ukraine policy is now tied to its own exposure to energy prices. The Prime Minister did not frame the energy ceasefire mainly as protection for Ukrainian civilians. He framed it as 'the quickest way' to get diesel back onto world markets without rewarding Russia.

In the same week, the government's response to the US–Russia agreement turned straight to energy prices and the cost of living. Meanwhile, sanctions now cover over 90% of Russia's oil-producing capacity. Squeezing Russian supply while relying on a US-brokered ceasefire to ease the resulting price pressure is a balancing act. If the ceasefire fails, the strain will show at the pump.

The scale of the support is also modest next to the rhetoric of 'as long as it takes'. The headline acceleration is £10 million of a £45 million missile package, set against a £1.6 billion multi-year commitment. Britain's leverage here is diplomatic, chiefly lobbying partners on the LNG ban, more than material.

The farm-and-fish grievances listed ahead of the UK–EU summit did not arise by accident. Full document checks on salmon, banned seed potatoes and shellfish, and export certificates costing up to £200 follow directly from the kind of trade relationship Britain chose a decade ago.

The summit can trim these costs. The more significant move is the Prime Minister's call for a 'serious dialogue' about long-term options. That is the first explicit signal from Downing Street in years that the post-Brexit settlement itself is open to revision. His careful hedging, 'the British public will be the boss', shows he knows how politically costly that conversation remains.

Two announcements in the same week pull in different directions. In Scotland, the Prime Minister tells Holyrood it is too centralised and that power should flow to regions and cities. In England, he is building Great British Railways: a single national body that brings operators back under one command, with Derby as its headquarters.

Putting the headquarters in Derby, for up to 450 staff, is regional rebalancing of jobs, not of decisions. The deeper problem it reveals is generational: under 7% of rail workers are under 25. That is the legacy of decades in which the industry stopped training its own people. Whether 600 apprenticeships over four years can close that gap matters more than where the head office sits.
